doc.title: Josephine Davies interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 14, 2025

chapter: Satori, spirituality and life outside music
title: Interests beyond music: reading, a philosophy and psychotherapy PhD
summary: Prompted by a Maria Schneider quote, she describes reading, her PhD in philosophy and psychotherapy, returning to music, and a mother who valued passion; Rowe cites Phil Woods.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You’ve led me to a quote I wrote down from this conversation I had years ago with Maria Schneider, who I know you’ve mentioned in your information. But she said, “One of the problems with musicians is they get so caught up in making records and going on to the next project. But what feeds the music? Music is fed by a deep and rich life so I think it’s really important to have other things in your life that you can do with equal love.”
Yup. Absolutely. Yeah. 100 percent I support that statement.
So do you have interests outside of your projects, which are numerous and varied?

Yes certainly. I’m an avid reader so I’m just always looking for – sometimes it’s new information but also I’m an avid reader of novels. Oddly enough I was just thinking about this yesterday. Somebody asked me one of those impossible questions – it’s an impossible, it’s a ridiculous question, but he said, “Would you rather go blind or deaf?” you know that old sort of mental acrobatics to try to imagine yourself into either of those

things which is of course impossible when you have both of those faculties. But it was a real struggle because I thought reading for me is as important as music in some ways, to really lose myself in a world that somebody else has imagined and then is giving to me through the means of the page, where I’m – as I’m reading their world I’m creating my own world. And I think there is something so fundamentally important about that for me that I’m not sure I could be a composer or a musician if I couldn’t experience that. I mean obviously people do and there are recordings in braille and all of that kind of thing, but as the question was being asked of me it just made me think about how important that is for me to sort of disappear into the other world. And I think part of my decision in my – when I turned 30 I sort of woke up one morning and decided that I really wanted to train as a psychotherapist. So I did a whole PhD in philosophy and psychotherapy. And when I got to the end of that, that was actually when I got my trio together. Because it opened up something for me that I was really passionate about. And then when I finished my doctorate I thought oh, I don’t want to do that anymore so I went hell for leather straight back into music as my dad was saying, “Well what did you do that for? That was so much money and now you’re not going to use it.” But I think it’s not about, it’s not necessarily about deciding that something is going to look that way in four years or five years, you just do – you make a commitment, you do the journey, take the journey, and then you find out where you are. And I was fortunate enough, you know, financially, to be able to go back into music and to earn my living that way rather than have to be a psychotherapist when I sort of lost the passion for the practice. But I still have a passion for the philosophy. So I think that was a real interest. And yeah, all the other things I do: yoga and walking and – I live by the sea now so I swim in the sea every day, which is getting cold. And yeah, relationships. I find all of that stuff absolutely essential for my nourishment. Otherwise I’m a bit starving when I come to music. So I would say Maria is hitting the nail on the head.
You did the opposite of what Phil Woods had said about young musicians. And his advice was well if you can be a doctor or a tenor player, be the doctor. And you went the other way.

Yeah. But I’m really – it’s got to be, obviously we live in a world where there are many limitations and constraints and we have to make it work in some way and it very much is about the possibilities that you have in life and also your dependents, who is relying on you, all of that stuff. But I think the question that – I was very fortunate enough to grow up with a mother whose – without explicitly stating it – letting me know that being – finding something passionate, finding something in your life that you’re passionate about will bring you great joy. Maybe grief as well. This is not about a spot of bland happiness but it’s – for me, particularly, it’s about finding something that is going to be endlessly
